opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a lot of the industry's attention went to action first, because that's the most visible part: an agent that writes code, opens a pull request, fixes a bug. It demos really well. But when you actually sit inside a large engineering organization, you realize that writing code is only a small fraction of what engineers spend their time on. Most of the work is understanding: figuring out how a system that's been built over ten years by hundreds of people actually fits together, why a particular decision was made, what will break if you touch something, who owns what.

And the quality of any action is bounded by the quality of the understanding behind it. If an agent doesn't have a deep model of your codebase, your infrastructure, your conventions, the history behind things, then even a very capable coding model will produce changes that look plausible but don't fit. You end up with a lot of code that a senior engineer has to carefully review and often rewrite, which doesn't really save anyone time.

So our view is that understanding is the foundation. If you can build a system that really comprehends an organization's software, the way your most tenured engineer does, then a lot of things open up. You can answer questions that currently interrupt your best people all day. You can onboard new engineers much faster. You can do reliable root-cause analysis when something breaks in production. And then action becomes much more trustworthy, because it's grounded in real context rather than pattern-matching on a local file.

There's also a technical angle. Understanding at scale is a genuinely hard research problem. Codebases are far larger than any context window, and the relevant knowledge is spread across code, tickets, docs, Slack threads, and people's heads. Building systems that can reason over all of that, and keep their understanding current as things change, is where I think a lot of the real leverage is. Action is in some sense the easier part once you've solved that.

r001.rationale: The response says actions become more trustworthy when grounded in a deep understanding of the organization’s software and context.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the industry’s focus on visible actions like writing code with engineers spending most of their time understanding systems.

r003.rationale: It says questions interrupt experienced engineers, but does not characterize collaboration as teammates asking one another about systems they do not understand.

r004.rationale: It calls organizational understanding a difficult technical problem, but does not identify it as an obstacle to superintelligence working within an organization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that when we started Reflection, the obvious thing everyone was excited about was action. Agents that write code, agents that open pull requests, agents that fix bugs. And that's genuinely valuable. But when you actually go sit with engineering teams, especially at larger organizations, you realize that the bottleneck usually isn't typing. The bottleneck is knowing what to type. It's knowing how the system actually works.

If you look at where senior engineers spend their time, a huge fraction of it is not writing code. It's answering questions. Why does this service behave this way? Who owns this? What happens downstream if I change this interface? Why was this decision made three years ago? That context lives in a very fragmented way. Some of it's in the code, some of it's in old design docs, some of it's in Slack threads, and a lot of it is just in people's heads. And when those people leave, it's gone.

So if you deploy an agent that's very good at acting but has a shallow understanding of that context, you get something that looks productive but is actually kind of dangerous. It'll make a change that's locally correct and globally wrong. And the engineer reviewing it now has to do all the understanding work anyway, except now they're doing it for code they didn't write, which is harder. You end up shifting the burden rather than removing it.

The other thing I'd say is that understanding compounds and action doesn't, really. If you build a system that deeply understands an organization's codebase, its history, its conventions, every action you take on top of that gets better. Whereas if you just get better at action without that foundation, you hit a ceiling pretty quickly. You can't reliably delegate work to someone who doesn't understand the thing they're working on, and the same is true for an agent.

And I think there's a trust dimension too. Engineering orgs don't adopt tools they don't trust, and trust comes from the agent being able to explain itself. When an agent can say, here's why this is structured this way, here's the history, here's what will break if you do that, people start to lean on it. That's the path to agents actually doing more autonomous work over time. You earn the right to act by first demonstrating that you understand.

r001.rationale: The response says agents with shallow organizational context can make locally correct but globally wrong changes, while deeper understanding makes actions better and more reliable.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the excitement around agents taking action with engineering teams’ main bottleneck being knowing how systems work, and describes senior engineers spending much of their time answering questions.

r003.rationale: It describes senior engineers answering questions about system behavior, ownership, downstream effects, and past decisions—implying teammates ask about systems they do not understand.

r004.rationale: The response presents organizational understanding as an obstacle to reliable AI-agent work, but does not identify it as an obstacle to superintelligence working within an organization.

astra-6.text:
Because action is only useful if you understand what you’re acting on. In an engineering organization, making a code change is often the easy part. The hard part is figuring out why the system works the way it does, which constraints matter, and what else might break if you change it.

An agent can produce a plausible patch without understanding the actual problem. And if you make that agent faster or give it more tools, you can end up amplifying the mistake. What you want is an agent that can build enough context to identify the right intervention—and recognize when it’s missing something and needs to ask a question.

So I’d put more emphasis on understanding because it makes action reliable. The goal isn’t just more activity. It’s less work for the engineers who otherwise have to check, correct, and undo that activity.

r001.rationale: The response says building enough context to identify the right intervention makes action reliable.

r002.rationale: It contrasts easy code changes with hard understanding, but does not identify AI development’s emphasis on action or engineers’ predominantly comprehension-oriented work.

r003.rationale: It mentions asking a question when context is missing, but not asking teammates about systems the agent does not understand.

r004.rationale: It discusses understanding engineering systems, but does not identify that as an obstacle to superintelligence working within an organization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think action is the visible part of the problem, so it gets a lot of attention. An agent writes code, opens a pull request, runs a test. But in an engineering organization, figuring out what to do is often harder than executing it. What does this service do? Why was it designed this way? Who depends on it? What constraint is missing from the ticket?

If you don’t understand that context, you can take a lot of actions without making progress. You might even produce something that passes the tests but solves the wrong problem.

So I’d put more emphasis on whether an agent can build an accurate picture of the system, recognize what it doesn’t know, and ask the question that resolves that uncertainty. Once it has that understanding, the action is much easier to specify—and much easier for a human to trust.

r001.rationale: It says agents that lack context may take actions without progress or solve the wrong problem, and that understanding makes actions easier to specify and trust.

r002.rationale: It contrasts attention to action with the difficulty of figuring out what to do, but does not state that engineers’ work is predominantly comprehension-oriented.

r003.rationale: It recommends asking questions to resolve uncertainty, but does not characterize engineering collaboration as asking teammates about systems one does not understand.

r004.rationale: It discusses understanding organizational context but does not identify that as an obstacle to superintelligence working within an organization.
